blocks.text: Nevertheless OEDMANN (in the Vermischten Sammlungen, fasc. 6, ch. 3) contends, on the sole authority of the Alexandrians, that ינשוף is the Tantalus Ibis of Linn., yet in such a way that in Esaj. XXXIV, 11. the Ibis niger is rather meant; O. G. TYCHSEN, ad Physiolog. Syr. Chapter 18, p. 105 and 178, also seems inclined to this opinion of Oedmann. To me the reliability of those translators in rendering the names of animals is highly suspect.
"Andreas Bellunensis explains Albasi [بازي] [bāzī] in Avicenna as the peregrine falcon." See ALDROVANDI, Ornithol. vol. 1, p. 461.
The باشق [bāshiq] of the Arabs is without doubt the Falco palumbarius of Linn. (vol. 1, part 1, p. 269, ed. Gmelin), the Autour of the French; see BUFFON, Hist. nat. des oiseaux, 1, p. 230.

Hubara: Otis flavicans, with very long whitish neck feathers striped with black, and large black flight feathers marked with a white spot near the middle, LINN. (vol. 1, part 2, p. 725, ed. Gmelin). Shaw, Itin. p. 162, 163, German trans., wished to exclude this bird from the genus of bustards, though he otherwise gave an accurate description of it. But BUFFON, Hist. des oiseaux, vol. 2, p. 59 (Le Houbara, ou petite Outarde huppée d' Afrique), claimed for it a place among the bustards. It lives in the deserts of Arabia; it feeds on shrubs and insects; by the variety of its flight and by stratagems it eludes the hawk that pursues it; it is the size of a capon, but longer, with the bill of a starling. I suspect, however, that the حباري [ḥubārá] of the Arabs comprises more than one species of bustard. Certainly everything that Abenbitar reports from Assariph in what follows fits the common great bustard. But what Damir relates below (p. 284) seems to suit the Tetrax better; see note 5, 6.

GALEN (book 3, de facult. medicam. ch. 20) says that the flesh of bustards is intermediate between that of cranes and that of geese, that is, less tough than crane's flesh but tougher than goose's. Belon (book 5, de Avib. ch. 3) says that the bustard is a delicate bird and is preferred at banquets to other birds.

From the book of CHARLES D'ARCUSSIA, a French nobleman, entitled Discours de chasse, Paris 1619, IOH. GOTTL. SCHNEIDER reports (in Commentart. ad Reliqua Friderici 2, p. 116) that the little bustard (Cannepetiere), after it has flown up, at once utters a whistle and empties its belly of excrement; from this habit Schneider thinks arose the story, also related by the emperor Frederick (book 1, ch. 56, p. 66, ed. Schneider), that the bustard wards off falcons by ejecting this excrement.

The Greeks seem to be reconciled with Damir thus: they speak of that species of bustard which for Linnaeus is the tarda avis (Trappe, Outarde), which because of the weight of its body makes only a very short flight; whereas Damir means the otis with smooth head and throat of Linn., the anas campestris of Gesner, the tetrax of Belon, the Cannepetiere of the French, which, flying close to the ground, extends its flight two or three hundred paces, but flies vigorously, and when it has come down to earth runs so swiftly that not even a man can follow it.
